        "text":"You're zeroing in on exactly the right thing. Both questions share an answer: **the API mirrors the JSON schema all the way down**, and the machinery already exists.\n\n## Q2 — `connect`'s argument is a connection entry, same shape as box JSON\n\nHere's the schema we already have on disk, from the test maps:\n\n```json\n\"connections\": [\n  { \"from_box\": \"src\", \"from_branch\": null,\n    \"to_box\": \"echo\", \"to_input\": \"x\" }\n]\n```\n\nEvery wire in SoraMech is already represented as one of these. **`to_input` is exactly the \"which port\" answer** — it's been the answer the whole time, just at compile-time rather than runtime. So `connect()` takes one (or many) of these objects:\n\n```\nconnect({from_box=A, from_branch=null, to_box=B, to_input=\"x\"})\nconnect({from_box=A, from_branch=null, to_box=B, to_input=\"x\"},\n        {from_box=A, from_branch=\"gt\", to_box=C, to_input=\"value\"},\n        {from_box=A, from_branch=\"lt\", to_box=D, to_input=\"value\"})\n```\n\nThe \"which port\" question is answered by **`to_input` being explicit in every connection entry**. No implicit-first-free magic, no separate \"port handle\" mechanism, no pair-style syntax that has to be remembered separately from the JSON shape. The shape on the wire (in the JSON file) and the shape in the API call are the same shape.\n\n`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`\nThis is the same principle as Q1.5 applied to a different artifact. **The schema is the API.** Every place we need a \"way to describe a box\" or \"way to describe a wire,\" the answer is \"use the JSON shape we already have on disk.\" It collapses two designs into one — and every future schema change updates the API for free.\n`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`\n\nVariadic falls out naturally — it's \"multiple connection entries in one call,\" exactly the way `connections[]` is an array on disk.\n\n## How do users *construct* these objects in code?\n\nThis is your \"how do we create the JSON schema, how do we edit its values\" question — practical, important. Different shape per language because the languages have different native data types:\n\n- **Lua:** table literal. Already idiomatic.\n  ```lua\n  soramech.connect({from_box=\"a\", from_branch=nil,\n                    to_box=\"b\", to_input=\"x\"})\n  ```\n\n- **C:** the verbose case. Three options ranked:\n  1. **Build a JSON string with a small varargs helper** — `connect_json(\"{\\\"from_box\\\":\\\"%s\\\",\\\"to_box\\\":\\\"%s\\\",\\\"to_input\\\":\\\"%s\\\"}\", \"a\", \"b\", \"x\")`. Ugly but works without any new infrastructure.\n  2. **Struct + builder helper** — `connection_t c = { .from_box=\"a\", .to_box=\"b\", .to_input=\"x\" }; soramech_connect(&c);` — uses C99 designated initializers, much cleaner.\n  3. **dkjson-style C JSON builder** — `cJSON *o = json_obj(); json_set(o, \"from_box\", \"a\"); ...; soramech_connect(o);` — most ergonomic, requires the runtime to expose a JSON-build API.\n  \n  Recommend option 2 (designated initializer struct) for the common case; option 1 falls back when the user has dynamic fields.\n\n- **Bash:** JSON strings. `soramech_connect '{\"from_box\":\"a\",\"to_box\":\"b\",\"to_input\":\"x\"}'`. Bash has no native dict; JSON strings are how it talks to everything anyway.\n\n## \"We output box return values to JSON sometimes. Could we use that machinery somehow?\" — Yes, the *same* machinery\n\nThis is the key insight you just pulled. Every language spec already implements `native_to_json` for the dual-ring wire format (issue 312) — that's how a Lua box's return value crosses into a C consumer. **Exactly the same callback** converts a Lua table the user built for create_box / connect into the JSON shape the runtime ingests. Concretely:\n\n```\n[user spec code]                 [language spec]              [runtime]\n  spec_table = {                 native_to_json               JSON object,\n    from_box = \"a\",          ──▶  (the same one used       ──▶ validate\n    to_box = \"b\",                  for wire crossings)         against schema,\n    to_input = \"x\"                                              instantiate\n  }                                                            connection\n  soramech.connect(spec_table)\n```\n\nThe benefits stack:\n\n- **No new callback** needed on the language spec. `native_to_json` is already there.\n- **Adding a new language costs nothing extra** for create_box / connect — anyone who implements the spec contract for the wire format gets metadata-construction for free.\n- **One validator** in the runtime: the box JSON schema validator already exists for `boxes/<id>.json` files at graph load. Reused as-is for runtime-constructed boxes.\n- **Persistence is trivial.** If `create_box` ever wants an \"also write this to disk\" option, it has the JSON in hand — `fwrite` to `boxes/<id>.json` and you're done.\n\nThe machinery you sensed should be reusable IS reusable. Same callback, same JSON, same validator, same on-disk format. The whole thing collapses to \"things in SoraMech are JSON; languages convert their native shapes to JSON; everything downstream consumes JSON.\"\n\nLet me write Q2 into the issue.",

          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"### Q2 — Which input port does `connect` target?\n\nA box has multiple input ports. `connect(from_box, to_box_a, ...)`\ndoesn't say which port on `to_box_a` receives the wire. Options:\n\n- **(a) Variadic of pairs:** `connect(from_box, {to_a, \"x\"}, {to_b, \"y\"})`\n  — explicit per destination, more typing.\n- **(b) Implicit first-free port:** the runtime picks the lowest-indexed\n  unwired input port on each destination. Cheap, surprising in mixed\n  cases.\n- **(c) Port-on-handle:** the handle returned by `create_box` carries\n  per-port sub-handles; `connect(from_box.output, to_box.input_x)`.\n  Verbose at call sites, unambiguous everywhere.",
          "new_string":"### Q2 — Which input port does `connect` target? — **RESOLVED: connection-entry shape from box JSON schema**\n\n**Resolution.** `connect`'s argument is **one (or many)\nstructured value(s) whose shape is exactly a connection entry\nfrom the box JSON schema's `connections[]` array**:\n\n```\nconnect({from_box=A, from_branch=null, to_box=B, to_input=\"x\"})\n```\n\nVariadic for multiple connections at once:\n\n```\nconnect({from_box=A, from_branch=null, to_box=B, to_input=\"x\"},\n        {from_box=A, from_branch=\"gt\",  to_box=C, to_input=\"value\"},\n        {from_box=A, from_branch=\"lt\",  to_box=D, to_input=\"value\"})\n```\n\nThe \"which port\" question is answered by **`to_input` being\nexplicit in every connection entry**. No implicit-first-free\nmagic, no pair-syntax that has to be remembered separately from\nthe JSON shape, no per-port sub-handles on the box handle. The\nshape on disk and the shape in the API call are identical.\n\n**Why this shape (consistent with Q1.5).** The schema is the\nAPI. Every place SoraMech needs a \"way to describe a box\" or a\n\"way to describe a wire,\" the same JSON shape we already have on\ndisk is what the API accepts. Two artifacts (the schema, the\nAPI) collapse to one artifact, and every future schema change\nupdates the API for free.\n\n**Construction in each language — `native_to_json` is the answer.**\n\nEach language spec already implements `native_to_json` for the\ndual-ring wire format (issue 312) — that's how a Lua box's\nreturn value crosses into a C consumer. The *same callback*\nconverts the user's spec-side value into the JSON shape the\nruntime ingests. No new spec contract; no new callback; adding\na new language gives self-construction for free.\n\n- **Lua:** table literal. Idiomatic, terse.\n  ```lua\n  soramech.connect({from_box = \"a\", from_branch = nil,\n                    to_box = \"b\", to_input = \"x\"})\n  ```\n- **C:** designated-initializer struct (`connection_t c = {.from_box=\"a\", ...};`)\n  for the common case; varargs JSON-string helper for dynamic\n  fields. The struct definition lives alongside the C spec's\n  header.\n- **Bash:** JSON string. Bash has no native dict; JSON strings\n  are how it talks to everything anyway.\n\n**Benefits that stack from machinery reuse:**\n\n- No new callback on the language spec — `native_to_json` is\n  already required for wire crossings.\n- One validator in the runtime — the box JSON schema validator\n  used for `boxes/<id>.json` files at graph load handles\n  runtime-constructed connections as-is.\n- Persistence is trivial — if `create_box` ever grows an \"also\n  write to disk\" option, the JSON is already in hand.\n- The connections inside a `create_box` call's structured value\n  (the box's own `connections[]` field) and standalone `connect()`\n  calls produce the same internal records.\n\n**What this resolution does NOT decide:** the precise validation\nerror policy when a `to_input` names a non-existent port (likely\nhard-crash per Q3 territory), and whether `connect()` accepts\nthe `from_box` as a handle from `create_box`, as the box's\nstring id, or both (likely both, since both can be resolved to\nthe same internal record). These fall under Q3 and Q4\nrespectively."
        },

    "newString":"### Q3 — Bool return versus hard-crash — **RESOLVED: hard-crash with reason**\n\n**Resolution.** `connect` returns nothing (`void`). On any\nfailure it aborts the program with a plain-English message\nnaming the boxes, the attempted wire, and what went wrong:\n\n```\nsoramech: cannot connect 'a' → 'b'.in_x\n  reason: 'b' has no input port named 'in_x'\n  available ports: 'count', 'label'\n```\n\nMatches the project-wide error policy in CLAUDE.md (\"prefer\nerror messages and breaking functionality over fallbacks\";\n\"nil checks are just asking for errors\"). A bool return invites\nsilent ignoring — if the user is calling `connect` they\nintend the wire to exist; any reason it doesn't is a bug worth\nsurfacing immediately, not a normal-flow result to branch on.\n\nThe corresponding `create_box` rule: failure to instantiate a\nbox (missing file, malformed schema, unknown spec language,\nduplicate id) is also a hard crash with reason. No box handle\nis returned for a failed creation — the program aborts before\nany caller has the chance to mis-use a null handle.\n\n### Q4 — What is the \"box handle\" actually? — **RESOLVED: auto-generated box_id string**\n\n**Resolution.** The handle returned by `create_box` is **a\nstring — the box's `id` field from the box JSON schema**. If\nthe caller's spec value supplied an explicit `id`, that string\nis returned. If `id` was omitted, the runtime mints an\nauto-generated UUID-style string (e.g.\n`auto_8f3c2a1e9b4d`) and uses it as the box's id.\n\nThe handle is therefore identical to the box_id used everywhere\nelse in the system: in `boxes/<id>.json` filenames, in the\n`from_box` / `to_box` fields of connection entries, in dispatch\nlog lines, in the run-output JSONL. There is no separate handle\ntype, no fast in-process pointer that has to be unwrapped at\nwire crossings, no struct carrying both an id and a pointer.\n\n**Why a string id (not an in-process pointer, not the function\nname).**\n\n- *Not an in-process pointer*: the handle has to survive being\n  passed to `connect()` from any worker, being persisted to\n  `tmp/last-run.jsonl`, and potentially being carried as a value\n  on a wire to another box. The cross-language wire format\n  explicitly forbids handles that back-route to a specific spec\n  (see `feedback_cross_language_pitfalls`). A string id has\n  none of those problems.\n- *Not the function name*: multiple boxes can run the same\n  function with different wiring, different input slot widths,\n  different external bindings. The id distinguishes them.\n- *Why UUID-style auto-generation*: when a runtime caller\n  constructs a box dynamically, they often don't have a\n  meaningful name in mind. Auto-generation removes the need to\n  invent one and removes the risk of collision with an\n  existing id. Callers who *do* want a meaningful name (for\n  log readability) can pass `id = \"my_planner_step_3\"`\n  themselves.\n\n**Internal lookup cost.** The dispatcher resolves\nbox_id → box record via a hash table (already needed for the\nexisting static graph load path). One hash lookup per `connect`\ncall, amortized to ~zero for the steady-state wire-push hot\npath (which holds a direct pointer cached at graph-build time).\nBox destruction (315) removes the hash entry as part of the\nrefcount-zero teardown.\n\n### Q5 — Does `create_box` trigger the build pipeline? — **RESOLVED: both, via a compile cache in tmp/**\n\n**Resolution.** Both runtime and compile-time paths exist, and\nthe runner stays ignorant of the compiler's internals by treating\nthe compiler as an external shell-out tool (which it already is:\n`scripts/soramech-compile.sh`).\n\n**The compile cache.** A directory under `tmp/` holds compiled\nartifacts keyed by a content hash of (source file + spec\nlanguage + relevant compile flags). When `create_box` resolves\na `ref` + `fn`:\n\n1. Compute the cache key from the source's contents and the\n   language spec.\n2. Look up the key in the cache.\n3. **Hit:** `dlopen` (or equivalent for the language) the cached\n   artifact and proceed.\n4. **Miss:** shell out to `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` with the\n   source path and target artifact path; wait for completion;\n   verify exit status; dlopen the freshly built artifact.\n\nThe runner never links the compiler, never imports\ncompiler-internal modules, never duplicates compiler logic. It\nonly knows \"if artifact X exists in the cache, use it; otherwise\nrun this script.\" The three-program separation in\n`project_soramech` (server / runner / editor) extends cleanly to\n\"runner treats compiler as external tool, same as it treats\nlanguage-spec subprocess binaries.\"\n\n**Compile-time precompilation as optimization.** When the\ncompile pipeline can statically determine that some\n`create_box(spec)` calls have constant `ref` + `fn` (e.g. the\nspec is a literal table in the caller's source), it can\npre-populate the cache during the compile step. Runtime calls\nto `create_box` with those refs hit the cache immediately, no\nshell-out latency. This is purely an optimization — correctness\ndoesn't depend on it. Defer the analysis pass until profiling\nshows the runtime compile-on-demand path is a bottleneck.\n\n**Cache invalidation.** Cache key includes source content hash,\nso changing a source file naturally produces a new key (and the\nold entry becomes garbage to be collected during run teardown).\nNo invalidation logic needed; content hashing is the\ninvalidation.\n\n**Why not pure runtime / pure compile-time:**\n\n- *Pure runtime*: every `create_box` call would pay shell-out\n  latency even for code that hasn't changed since the previous\n  run. Wasteful in tight loops or hot planner boxes.\n- *Pure compile-time*: dynamic `create_box` calls (where `ref`\n  comes from a runtime value, e.g. a planner box choosing what\n  pipeline to construct based on LLM output) can't be analyzed\n  ahead of time. Forbidding them gives up the use case that\n  motivates self-construction in the first place.\n\nThe cache makes both paths cheap when they apply and removes the\nneed to pick one.",

    "oldString":"### Q3 — Bool return versus hard-crash\n\nCLAUDE.md says \"prefer error messages and breaking functionality\nover fallbacks\" and \"nil checks are just asking for errors.\" A\nbool return on `connect` is exactly the shape that invites silent\nignoring. Two paths:\n\n- **(a) Keep bool.** The caller is expected to branch on it. Matches\n  the user's draft.\n- **(b) Hard-crash with reason.** `connect` returns nothing; on any\n  failure it aborts the program with a plain-English message\n  (\"can't connect box X to box Y: Y has no free input ports\").\n  Matches the project-wide error policy elsewhere.\n\n### Q4 — What is the \"box handle\" actually?\n\nThe user wrote \"pointer to the box.\" In a single-process runner the\nliteral pointer works, but it can't survive wire crossings or be\npassed across the cross-language JSON wire (the wire format forbids\nhandles that back-route to the owning spec). Options:\n\n- **(a) Stable string id** (the existing `box_id` from the JSON\n  schema). Survives serialization. Slower lookup in the dispatch\n  layer.\n- **(b) In-process `$ref` sentinel.** Fast in the calling spec,\n  must be unwrapped before crossing a language boundary.\n- **(c) Both:** the handle is a small struct carrying both the\n  fast pointer and the durable id; the wire layer keeps only the\n  id when it crosses.\n\n### Q5 — Does `create_box` trigger the build pipeline?\n\nThe user said \"compile it (if necessary) and other map-wide tasks.\"\nThe build pipeline (issues 217–222) currently lives on the server /\ncompile-button side. If `create_box` runs at runtime, the runner\ngains a dependency on the compiler. That crosses the program-\nseparation boundary documented in `project_soramech`:\n\"Server never knows about runner. Runner never knows about server.\nMap directory format is the only shared contract.\"\n\nEither the runner gains the compiler as a library (changing the\nthree-program separation), or `create_box` requires the source to\nbe pre-compiled and merely *registers* the resulting artifact\n(simpler, but the user has to do the build step separately)."
  },

        "name":"Edit",
        "input":{
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/319-builtin-library-for-map-self-construction.md",
          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"### Q3 — Bool return versus hard-crash\n\nCLAUDE.md says \"prefer error messages and breaking functionality\nover fallbacks\" and \"nil checks are just asking for errors.\" A\nbool return on `connect` is exactly the shape that invites silent\nignoring. Two paths:\n\n- **(a) Keep bool.** The caller is expected to branch on it. Matches\n  the user's draft.\n- **(b) Hard-crash with reason.** `connect` returns nothing; on any\n  failure it aborts the program with a plain-English message\n  (\"can't connect box X to box Y: Y has no free input ports\").\n  Matches the project-wide error policy elsewhere.\n\n### Q4 — What is the \"box handle\" actually?\n\nThe user wrote \"pointer to the box.\" In a single-process runner the\nliteral pointer works, but it can't survive wire crossings or be\npassed across the cross-language JSON wire (the wire format forbids\nhandles that back-route to the owning spec). Options:\n\n- **(a) Stable string id** (the existing `box_id` from the JSON\n  schema). Survives serialization. Slower lookup in the dispatch\n  layer.\n- **(b) In-process `$ref` sentinel.** Fast in the calling spec,\n  must be unwrapped before crossing a language boundary.\n- **(c) Both:** the handle is a small struct carrying both the\n  fast pointer and the durable id; the wire layer keeps only the\n  id when it crosses.\n\n### Q5 — Does `create_box` trigger the build pipeline?\n\nThe user said \"compile it (if necessary) and other map-wide tasks.\"\nThe build pipeline (issues 217–222) currently lives on the server /\ncompile-button side. If `create_box` runs at runtime, the runner\ngains a dependency on the compiler. That crosses the program-\nseparation boundary documented in `project_soramech`:\n\"Server never knows about runner. Runner never knows about server.\nMap directory format is the only shared contract.\"\n\nEither the runner gains the compiler as a library (changing the\nthree-program separation), or `create_box` requires the source to\nbe pre-compiled and merely *registers* the resulting artifact\n(simpler, but the user has to do the build step separately).",
          "new_string":"### Q3 — Bool return versus hard-crash — **RESOLVED: hard-crash with reason**\n\n**Resolution.** `connect` returns nothing (`void`). On any\nfailure it aborts the program with a plain-English message\nnaming the boxes, the attempted wire, and what went wrong:\n\n```\nsoramech: cannot connect 'a' → 'b'.in_x\n  reason: 'b' has no input port named 'in_x'\n  available ports: 'count', 'label'\n```\n\nMatches the project-wide error policy in CLAUDE.md (\"prefer\nerror messages and breaking functionality over fallbacks\";\n\"nil checks are just asking for errors\"). A bool return invites\nsilent ignoring — if the user is calling `connect` they\nintend the wire to exist; any reason it doesn't is a bug worth\nsurfacing immediately, not a normal-flow result to branch on.\n\nThe corresponding `create_box` rule: failure to instantiate a\nbox (missing file, malformed schema, unknown spec language,\nduplicate id) is also a hard crash with reason. No box handle\nis returned for a failed creation — the program aborts before\nany caller has the chance to mis-use a null handle.\n\n### Q4 — What is the \"box handle\" actually? — **RESOLVED: auto-generated box_id string**\n\n**Resolution.** The handle returned by `create_box` is **a\nstring — the box's `id` field from the box JSON schema**. If\nthe caller's spec value supplied an explicit `id`, that string\nis returned. If `id` was omitted, the runtime mints an\nauto-generated UUID-style string (e.g.\n`auto_8f3c2a1e9b4d`) and uses it as the box's id.\n\nThe handle is therefore identical to the box_id used everywhere\nelse in the system: in `boxes/<id>.json` filenames, in the\n`from_box` / `to_box` fields of connection entries, in dispatch\nlog lines, in the run-output JSONL. There is no separate handle\ntype, no fast in-process pointer that has to be unwrapped at\nwire crossings, no struct carrying both an id and a pointer.\n\n**Why a string id (not an in-process pointer, not the function\nname).**\n\n- *Not an in-process pointer*: the handle has to survive being\n  passed to `connect()` from any worker, being persisted to\n  `tmp/last-run.jsonl`, and potentially being carried as a value\n  on a wire to another box. The cross-language wire format\n  explicitly forbids handles that back-route to a specific spec\n  (see `feedback_cross_language_pitfalls`). A string id has\n  none of those problems.\n- *Not the function name*: multiple boxes can run the same\n  function with different wiring, different input slot widths,\n  different external bindings. The id distinguishes them.\n- *Why UUID-style auto-generation*: when a runtime caller\n  constructs a box dynamically, they often don't have a\n  meaningful name in mind. Auto-generation removes the need to\n  invent one and removes the risk of collision with an\n  existing id. Callers who *do* want a meaningful name (for\n  log readability) can pass `id = \"my_planner_step_3\"`\n  themselves.\n\n**Internal lookup cost.** The dispatcher resolves\nbox_id → box record via a hash table (already needed for the\nexisting static graph load path). One hash lookup per `connect`\ncall, amortized to ~zero for the steady-state wire-push hot\npath (which holds a direct pointer cached at graph-build time).\nBox destruction (315) removes the hash entry as part of the\nrefcount-zero teardown.\n\n### Q5 — Does `create_box` trigger the build pipeline? — **RESOLVED: both, via a compile cache in tmp/**\n\n**Resolution.** Both runtime and compile-time paths exist, and\nthe runner stays ignorant of the compiler's internals by treating\nthe compiler as an external shell-out tool (which it already is:\n`scripts/soramech-compile.sh`).\n\n**The compile cache.** A directory under `tmp/` holds compiled\nartifacts keyed by a content hash of (source file + spec\nlanguage + relevant compile flags). When `create_box` resolves\na `ref` + `fn`:\n\n1. Compute the cache key from the source's contents and the\n   language spec.\n2. Look up the key in the cache.\n3. **Hit:** `dlopen` (or equivalent for the language) the cached\n   artifact and proceed.\n4. **Miss:** shell out to `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` with the\n   source path and target artifact path; wait for completion;\n   verify exit status; dlopen the freshly built artifact.\n\nThe runner never links the compiler, never imports\ncompiler-internal modules, never duplicates compiler logic. It\nonly knows \"if artifact X exists in the cache, use it; otherwise\nrun this script.\" The three-program separation in\n`project_soramech` (server / runner / editor) extends cleanly to\n\"runner treats compiler as external tool, same as it treats\nlanguage-spec subprocess binaries.\"\n\n**Compile-time precompilation as optimization.** When the\ncompile pipeline can statically determine that some\n`create_box(spec)` calls have constant `ref` + `fn` (e.g. the\nspec is a literal table in the caller's source), it can\npre-populate the cache during the compile step. Runtime calls\nto `create_box` with those refs hit the cache immediately, no\nshell-out latency. This is purely an optimization — correctness\ndoesn't depend on it. Defer the analysis pass until profiling\nshows the runtime compile-on-demand path is a bottleneck.\n\n**Cache invalidation.** Cache key includes source content hash,\nso changing a source file naturally produces a new key (and the\nold entry becomes garbage to be collected during run teardown).\nNo invalidation logic needed; content hashing is the\ninvalidation.\n\n**Why not pure runtime / pure compile-time:**\n\n- *Pure runtime*: every `create_box` call would pay shell-out\n  latency even for code that hasn't changed since the previous\n  run. Wasteful in tight loops or hot planner boxes.\n- *Pure compile-time*: dynamic `create_box` calls (where `ref`\n  comes from a runtime value, e.g. a planner box choosing what\n  pipeline to construct based on LLM output) can't be analyzed\n  ahead of time. Forbidding them gives up the use case that\n  motivates self-construction in the first place.\n\nThe cache makes both paths cheap when they apply and removes the\nneed to pick one."
        },
        "caller":{
          "type":"direct"
        },
        "id":"toolu_012ZBsHamJreCgWGAst46oK2",
        "type":"tool_use"
      }]

      "content":"    }\n    /* Slice 5 of issue 312: there's now a single invoke entry point.\n     * The per-input `input_native[]` array and the per-call\n     * `output_native` flag carry the same-language-vs-cross-language\n     * information the old `invoke_native` / `invoke_json` callback\n     * split was meant to encode. The bridges (`native_to_json`,\n     * `json_to_native`) stay on the spec interface for the few\n     * places that consume them directly. */\n    lang_invoke_fn fn = spec->invoke;\n    if (!fn) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"dispatch: '%s' spec missing invoke\\n\", b->id);\n        return -1;\n    }\n    void *handle = pool_current_worker\n        ? pool_current_worker->handles[b->spec_idx]\n        : NULL;\n    if (!handle) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"dispatch: '%s' worker handle for spec[%d] is NULL\\n\",\n                b->id, b->spec_idx);\n        return -1;\n    }\n\n    /* Read inputs. */\n    int n = b->n_inputs;\n    char        *bufs[16]       = {0};\n    ua_chunk_t  *buf_chunks[16] = {0};\n    const void  *datas[16]      = {0};\n    int          sizes[16]      = {0};\n    int          input_native[16] = {0};\n    if (n > (int)(sizeof bufs / sizeof bufs[0])) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"dispatch: '%s' has %d inputs (cap = %d)\\n\",\n                b->id, n, (int)(sizeof bufs / sizeof bufs[0]));\n        return -1;\n    }\n    int failed = 0;\n    int n_present = read_inputs(ctx, b, bufs, buf_chunks, datas, sizes,\n                                input_native,\n                                ctx->default_out_capacity, &failed);\n    if (failed) {\n        release_inputs(ctx, n, bufs, buf_chunks);\n        return -1;\n    }\n\n    /* Verbose: emit the input payloads now, before the spec runs. */\n    emit_input_events(ctx, task_id, bufs, sizes, n_present);\n\n    /* Resolve the box's source file relative to map_dir. */\n    char *ref_path = b->ref ? resolve_path(ctx, b->ref) : NULL;\n\n    /* Slice 4.5 of issue 312: pick the box's output format once, at\n     * call time. If every outgoing wire goes to a consumer in this\n     * box's own language, the spec writes its fast native form;\n     * otherwise it writes JSON so the cross-language consumers can\n     * parse it. The decision is per-call, not per-edge — the spec\n     * writes once, the push then routes that one format to every\n     * consumer uniformly. Same-language consumers in a\n     * mixed-fan-out box eat the JSON cost as the price of having a\n     * cross-language sibling; the precision tradeoff is captured in\n     * issue 312's \"Resolved design choice\" section. */\n    int output_native = all_wires_native(b);\n\n    int rc = fn(handle, b, ref_path ? ref_path : b->ref, b->fn,\n                datas, sizes, input_native, n_present,\n                output_native,\n                out_buf, out_capacity, out_size);\n    free(ref_path);\n    release_inputs(ctx, n, bufs, buf_chunks);\n    return rc;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ do_write_box() — write `value` input to `path`, emit \"true\" */\n/* Convention (issue 229): inputs are named \"path\" (string) and\n * \"value\" (bytes). Either may carry a static literal supplied\n * via dispatch_push_literals.\n *\n * On success, the box pushes the boolean string `\"true\"` to its\n * outgoing connections. A `write` box with no downstream wire\n * still produces the boolean; the dispatch fans to zero consumers\n * and the value is discarded (unwired-output rule). */\nstatic int do_write_box(dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, const box_t *b, int task_id,\n                        char *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size)\n{\n    char        *bufs[16]       = {0};\n    ua_chunk_t  *buf_chunks[16] = {0};\n    const void  *datas[16]      = {0};\n    int          sizes[16]      = {0};\n    int failed = 0;\n    /* do_write_box doesn't invoke a language spec — it's a dispatch\n     * primitive that writes a file. The per-input native flag isn't\n     * meaningful here, so pass NULL. */\n    int n_present = read_inputs(ctx, b, bufs, buf_chunks, datas, sizes,\n                                /*input_native=*/NULL,\n                                ctx->default_out_capacity, &failed);\n    emit_input_events(ctx, task_id, bufs, sizes, n_present);\n    int path_idx = -1, value_idx = -1;\n    for (int i = 0; i < b->n_inputs; i++) {\n        if (strcmp(b->inputs[i].name, \"path\")  == 0) path_idx  = i;\n        if (strcmp(b->inputs[i].name, \"value\") == 0) value_idx = i;\n    }\n    if (failed || path_idx < 0 || value_idx < 0\n            || path_idx >= n_present || value_idx >= n_present) {\n        release_inputs(ctx, b->n_inputs, bufs, buf_chunks);\n        return -1;\n    }\n    /* Make NUL-terminated copy of the path. */\n    char *path = malloc((size_t)sizes[path_idx] + 1);\n    if (!path) {\n        release_inputs(ctx, b->n_inputs, bufs, buf_chunks);\n        return -1;\n    }\n    memcpy(path, datas[path_idx], (size_t)sizes[path_idx]);\n    path[sizes[path_idx]] = '\\0';\n\n    char *full = resolve_path(ctx, path);\n    free(path);\n    if (!full) {\n        release_inputs(ctx, b->n_inputs, bufs, buf_chunks);\n        return -1;\n    }\n\n    FILE *fp = fopen(full, \"wb\");\n    free(full);\n    int rc = 0;\n    if (!fp) rc = -1;\n    else {\n        size_t want = (size_t)sizes[value_idx];\n        if (fwrite(datas[value_idx], 1, want, fp) != want) rc = -1;\n        fclose(fp);\n    }\n    release_inputs(ctx, b->n_inputs, bufs, buf_chunks);\n\n    if (rc == 0 && out_buf && out_capacity >= 4) {\n        memcpy(out_buf, \"true\", 4);\n        *out_size = 4;\n    } else {\n        *out_size = 0;\n    }\n    return rc;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ dispatch_action() — the pool action body */\nvoid dispatch_action(void *arg)\n{\n    dispatch_task_t *t = (dispatch_task_t *)arg;\n    if (!t) return;\n    dispatch_ctx_t *ctx = (dispatch_ctx_t *)t->ctx;\n    const box_t *b = graph_box(ctx->graph, t->box_id);\n\n    atomic_fetch_add_explicit(&ctx->tasks_dispatched, 1, memory_order_relaxed);\n\n    int task_id    = t->task_id;\n    int worker_idx = pool_current_worker ? pool_current_worker->thread_idx : -1;\n\n    long start_us = mono_us();\n    if (ctx->events)\n        event_queue_task_start(ctx->events, now_secs(), task_id, worker_idx);\n\n    int out_size = 0;"

        "content":"780\t    }\n781\t    /* Slice 5 of issue 312: there's now a single invoke entry point.\n782\t     * The per-input `input_native[]` array and the per-call\n783\t     * `output_native` flag carry the same-language-vs-cross-language\n784\t     * information the old `invoke_native` / `invoke_json` callback\n785\t     * split was meant to encode. The bridges (`native_to_json`,\n786\t     * `json_to_native`) stay on the spec interface for the few\n787\t     * places that consume them directly. */\n788\t    lang_invoke_fn fn = spec->invoke;\n789\t    if (!fn) {\n790\t        fprintf(stderr, \"dispatch: '%s' spec missing invoke\\n\", b->id);\n791\t        return -1;\n792\t    }\n793\t    void *handle = pool_current_worker\n794\t        ? pool_current_worker->handles[b->spec_idx]\n795\t        : NULL;\n796\t    if (!handle) {\n797\t        fprintf(stderr, \"dispatch: '%s' worker handle for spec[%d] is NULL\\n\",\n798\t                b->id, b->spec_idx);\n799\t        return -1;\n800\t    }\n801\t\n802\t    /* Read inputs. */\n803\t    int n = b->n_inputs;\n804\t    char        *bufs[16]       = {0};\n805\t    ua_chunk_t  *buf_chunks[16] = {0};\n806\t    const void  *datas[16]      = {0};\n807\t    int          sizes[16]      = {0};\n808\t    int          input_native[16] = {0};\n809\t    if (n > (int)(sizeof bufs / sizeof bufs[0])) {\n810\t        fprintf(stderr, \"dispatch: '%s' has %d inputs (cap = %d)\\n\",\n811\t                b->id, n, (int)(sizeof bufs / sizeof bufs[0]));\n812\t        return -1;\n813\t    }\n814\t    int failed = 0;\n815\t    int n_present = read_inputs(ctx, b, bufs, buf_chunks, datas, sizes,\n816\t                                input_native,\n817\t                                ctx->default_out_capacity, &failed);\n818\t    if (failed) {\n819\t        release_inputs(ctx, n, bufs, buf_chunks);\n820\t        return -1;\n821\t    }\n822\t\n823\t    /* Verbose: emit the input payloads now, before the spec runs. */\n824\t    emit_input_events(ctx, task_id, bufs, sizes, n_present);\n825\t\n826\t    /* Resolve the box's source file relative to map_dir. */\n827\t    char *ref_path = b->ref ? resolve_path(ctx, b->ref) : NULL;\n828\t\n829\t    /* Slice 4.5 of issue 312: pick the box's output format once, at\n830\t     * call time. If every outgoing wire goes to a consumer in this\n831\t     * box's own language, the spec writes its fast native form;\n832\t     * otherwise it writes JSON so the cross-language consumers can\n833\t     * parse it. The decision is per-call, not per-edge — the spec\n834\t     * writes once, the push then routes that one format to every\n835\t     * consumer uniformly. Same-language consumers in a\n836\t     * mixed-fan-out box eat the JSON cost as the price of having a\n837\t     * cross-language sibling; the precision tradeoff is captured in\n838\t     * issue 312's \"Resolved design choice\" section. */\n839\t    int output_native = all_wires_native(b);\n840\t\n841\t    int rc = fn(handle, b, ref_path ? ref_path : b->ref, b->fn,\n842\t                datas, sizes, input_native, n_present,\n843\t                output_native,\n844\t                out_buf, out_capacity, out_size);\n845\t    free(ref_path);\n846\t    release_inputs(ctx, n, bufs, buf_chunks);\n847\t    return rc;\n848\t}\n849\t/* }}} */\n850\t\n851\t/* {{{ do_write_box() — write `value` input to `path`, emit \"true\" */\n852\t/* Convention (issue 229): inputs are named \"path\" (string) and\n853\t * \"value\" (bytes). Either may carry a static literal supplied\n854\t * via dispatch_push_literals.\n855\t *\n856\t * On success, the box pushes the boolean string `\"true\"` to its\n857\t * outgoing connections. A `write` box with no downstream wire\n858\t * still produces the boolean; the dispatch fans to zero consumers\n859\t * and the value is discarded (unwired-output rule). */\n860\tstatic int do_write_box(dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, const box_t *b, int task_id,\n861\t                        char *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size)\n862\t{\n863\t    char        *bufs[16]       = {0};\n864\t    ua_chunk_t  *buf_chunks[16] = {0};\n865\t    const void  *datas[16]      = {0};\n866\t    int          sizes[16]      = {0};\n867\t    int failed = 0;\n868\t    /* do_write_box doesn't invoke a language spec — it's a dispatch\n869\t     * primitive that writes a file. The per-input native flag isn't\n870\t     * meaningful here, so pass NULL. */\n871\t    int n_present = read_inputs(ctx, b, bufs, buf_chunks, datas, sizes,\n872\t                                /*input_native=*/NULL,\n873\t                                ctx->default_out_capacity, &failed);\n874\t    emit_input_events(ctx, task_id, bufs, sizes, n_present);\n875\t    int path_idx = -1, value_idx = -1;\n876\t    for (int i = 0; i < b->n_inputs; i++) {\n877\t        if (strcmp(b->inputs[i].name, \"path\")  == 0) path_idx  = i;\n878\t        if (strcmp(b->inputs[i].name, \"value\") == 0) value_idx = i;\n879\t    }\n880\t    if (failed || path_idx < 0 || value_idx < 0\n881\t            || path_idx >= n_present || value_idx >= n_present) {\n882\t        release_inputs(ctx, b->n_inputs, bufs, buf_chunks);\n883\t        return -1;\n884\t    }\n885\t    /* Make NUL-terminated copy of the path. */\n886\t    char *path = malloc((size_t)sizes[path_idx] + 1);\n887\t    if (!path) {\n888\t        release_inputs(ctx, b->n_inputs, bufs, buf_chunks);\n889\t        return -1;\n890\t    }\n891\t    memcpy(path, datas[path_idx], (size_t)sizes[path_idx]);\n892\t    path[sizes[path_idx]] = '\\0';\n893\t\n894\t    char *full = resolve_path(ctx, path);\n895\t    free(path);\n896\t    if (!full) {\n897\t        release_inputs(ctx, b->n_inputs, bufs, buf_chunks);\n898\t        return -1;\n899\t    }\n900\t\n901\t    FILE *fp = fopen(full, \"wb\");\n902\t    free(full);\n903\t    int rc = 0;\n904\t    if (!fp) rc = -1;\n905\t    else {\n906\t        size_t want = (size_t)sizes[value_idx];\n907\t        if (fwrite(datas[value_idx], 1, want, fp) != want) rc = -1;\n908\t        fclose(fp);\n909\t    }\n910\t    release_inputs(ctx, b->n_inputs, bufs, buf_chunks);\n911\t\n912\t    if (rc == 0 && out_buf && out_capacity >= 4) {\n913\t        memcpy(out_buf, \"true\", 4);\n914\t        *out_size = 4;\n915\t    } else {\n916\t        *out_size = 0;\n917\t    }\n918\t    return rc;\n919\t}\n920\t/* }}} */\n921\t\n922\t/* {{{ dispatch_action() — the pool action body */\n923\tvoid dispatch_action(void *arg)\n924\t{\n925\t    dispatch_task_t *t = (dispatch_task_t *)arg;\n926\t    if (!t) return;\n927\t    dispatch_ctx_t *ctx = (dispatch_ctx_t *)t->ctx;\n928\t    const box_t *b = graph_box(ctx->graph, t->box_id);\n929\t\n930\t    atomic_fetch_add_explicit(&ctx->tasks_dispatched, 1, memory_order_relaxed);\n931\t\n932\t    int task_id    = t->task_id;\n933\t    int worker_idx = pool_current_worker ? pool_current_worker->thread_idx : -1;\n934\t\n935\t    long start_us = mono_us();\n936\t    if (ctx->events)\n937\t        event_queue_task_start(ctx->events, now_secs(), task_id, worker_idx);\n938\t\n939\t    int out_size = 0;",
        "tool_use_id":"toolu_01Acc6VqsPzUANhKkjRqWjKR",
        "type":"tool_result"

          "content":"# 319a — Remove dispatch input cap (prerequisite for create_box)\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Parent issue\nThis is the first slice of issue 319 (built-in library for map\nself-construction). The full design lives in 319; this sub-issue\nimplements the prerequisite from 319's \"Prerequisite — remove the\ndispatch input cap\" section.\n\n## Current behavior\n\n`src/012-dispatch.c` allocates five parallel stack arrays of\nfixed size 16 inside the per-call invocation path (`invoke_box_impl`,\naround lines 804–808, and the parallel set in `do_write_box`,\naround lines 863–866):\n\n```c\nchar        *bufs[16]         = {0};\nua_chunk_t  *buf_chunks[16]   = {0};\nconst void  *datas[16]        = {0};\nint          sizes[16]        = {0};\nint          input_native[16] = {0};\n```\n\nA box with more than 16 inputs hits a hard error (`return -1`)\nfrom the dispatcher with the message `'<id>' has N inputs\n(cap = 16)`. The error is loud, but the cap is arbitrary — it\nexists because someone needed a stack array and picked a number\nthat seemed big enough.\n\nFive additional sites use `char branch[24]` to format\n`\"out_%u\"` strings via `snprintf` (dispatch.c lines 629, 647,\n678, 708, 739). The formatted string is at most 15 bytes\n(`\"out_4294967295\\0\"`), so 24 never truncates, but the\nconstant is arbitrary and the format-string convention is\nimplicit.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nThe five parallel input arrays size themselves at call time to\nthe box's actual input count, with a sanity ceiling that lets us\nreject pathological values (a box with a million inputs is almost\ncertainly a graph-loader bug, not a real use case). No fixed\ncap of 16. A box with 17 inputs runs the same as a box with 7.\n\nThe five branch buffers use a single named constant\n`MAX_BRANCH_NAME` whose size is provably sufficient for the\n`\"out_%u\"` format. The constant lives at file scope so any\nfuture format-string change touches one definition.\n\n## Suggested implementation\n\n1. **Choose the array-sizing approach.** Two acceptable shapes:\n   - **VLA**: `char *bufs[n > 0 ? n : 1]; memset(bufs, 0, sizeof bufs);`\n     for each of the five arrays. C99 standard. Zero stack cost\n     for typical n. Cost: each array gets a tiny init loop;\n     zero-size VLAs are UB so the `n > 0` guard is required.\n   - **SBO**: keep the `[16]` stack arrays as a fast path; fall\n     back to `calloc` when `n > 16`; free at end. Common case\n     pays zero overhead; rare case pays five small allocations.\n\n   Recommended: **VLA** for simplicity. The codebase is C and\n   has no aversion to C99 features. SBO is a fallback if profiling\n   ever shows VLA stack pressure.\n\n2. **Add a sanity ceiling.** Hard-cap n at 4096 (or similar large\n   value). Keep the existing error path; just update the message\n   to name the new ceiling and call out that it's a sanity guard,\n   not a feature limit.\n\n3. **Apply the same change in `do_write_box`** — the parallel\n   arrays there have the same shape, the same cap, and need the\n   same fix.\n\n4. **Introduce `MAX_BRANCH_NAME`** at the top of `dispatch.c`\n   (or in a shared header if it's referenced elsewhere). Replace\n   the five `char branch[24]` / `char want[24]` declarations with\n   `char branch[MAX_BRANCH_NAME]`. Value chosen so that\n   `\"out_4294967295\\0\"` (15 bytes) fits with margin (16 or 32).\n\n5. **Test.** Either:\n   - Add a unit test under `tests/319a-dispatch-vla-test.c` that\n     constructs a box record with > 16 inputs and runs it through\n     the dispatch invocation path, or\n   - Add a test map under `tests/maps/319a-many-inputs/` with a\n     box whose function accepts 20 inputs, exercised by the\n     existing test runner.\n\n   The first option is more isolated; the second is more\n   end-to-end. Probably do both — the unit test catches the change,\n   the map confirms nothing else along the path silently caps.\n\n6. **Build the full test suite** and confirm no existing tests\n   regress.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — the five-array allocation in\n  `invoke_box_impl()` and `do_write_box()`; the five `branch[24]`\n  sites.\n\n## Not in scope for this sub-issue\n\n- Slot store growth (319b).\n- Box id generator / compile cache (319c).\n- The `create_box` / `connect` runtime built-ins themselves\n  (319d, 319e).\n"
        },
        "caller":{
          "type":"direct"
        },
        "id":"toolu_01U4eVJb1rm7cUYNmr4H2cfz",
        "type":"tool_use"
      }]

          "content":"# 319b — Slot store growth primitive\n\n## Status\nopen — planning stub. Full design in parent issue 319's \"Q1\"\nresolution.\n\n## Parent issue\nSub-issue of 319 (built-in library for map self-construction).\nThe design for this slice is fully specified in 319's \"Q1 —\nWhen does the new box exist?\" resolution section.\n\n## Current behavior\n\n`src/009-slot-store.{c,h}` allocates all slots at graph load.\nThe store has no growth primitive; slot pointers are stable for\nthe run because the array never moves. The header explicitly\nstates: \"Lifetime is the run. Slots are freed when the store is\ndestroyed at the end of the run.\"\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nThe slot store grows at runtime via a three-layer chunked-append\n+ RCU-swap structure (see 319's Q1 resolution for the full\ndiagram and rationale). Slots themselves never move; chunks\nthemselves never move; only the top-level index array swaps when\nit fills, and the swap uses double-buffer-with-defer-free.\n\n## Suggested implementation\n\nTo be expanded when this sub-issue is picked up. The design is\nalready final in 319.\n\nTouches: `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}`, `tests/009-slot-store-test.c`.\n\n## Not in scope\n\nPer-slot ring buffer growth (separate concern — same double-buffer\npattern under the per-slot lock, but a different code path).\n"

Full design in parent issue 319's \"Q1\"\nresolution.\n\n## Parent issue\nSub-issue of 319 (built-in library for map self-construction).\nThe design for this slice is fully specified in 319's \"Q1 —\nWhen does the new box exist?\" resolution section.\n\n## Current behavior\n\n`src/009-slot-store.{c,h}` allocates all slots at graph load.\nThe store has no growth primitive; slot pointers are stable for\nthe run because the array never moves. The header explicitly\nstates: \"Lifetime is the run. Slots are freed when the store is\ndestroyed at the end of the run.\"\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nThe slot store grows at runtime via a three-layer chunked-append\n+ RCU-swap structure (see 319's Q1 resolution for the full\ndiagram and rationale). Slots themselves never move; chunks\nthemselves never move; only the top-level index array swaps when\nit fills, and the swap uses double-buffer-with-defer-free.\n\n## Suggested implementation\n\nTo be expanded when this sub-issue is picked up. The design is\nalready final in 319.\n\nTouches: `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}`, `tests/009-slot-store-test.c`.\n\n## Not in scope\n\nPer-slot ring buffer growth (separate concern — same double-buffer\npattern under the per-slot lock, but a different code path).\n"
  },

Combines two small independent utilities that\nboth gate `create_box`:\n\n- **Box id generator** — auto-generates UUID-style box_id strings\n  for `create_box` callers who don't supply an explicit `id`.\n  Design: 319 Q4.\n- **Compile cache** — content-hash-keyed lookup under `tmp/`,\n  shell-out to `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` on cache miss,\n  dlopen the resulting artifact. Preserves the runner-doesn't-know-\n  about-compiler separation. Design: 319 Q5.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n- A `box_id_generate()` utility returns a string like\n  `auto_8f3c2a1e9b4d`. Collision-free within a run.\n- A `compile_cache_resolve(source_path, lang_spec)` utility\n  returns a dlopen-ready artifact path. Cache hit returns\n  immediately; cache miss invokes the compile script and waits.\n\n## Suggested implementation\n\nTo be expanded when picked up. Both utilities are independent of\nthe slot store work and can land before 319b if convenient.\n"

      "content":"/* src/012-dispatch.c — task dispatch layer, implementation.\n *\n * The pool action does five things, in order:\n *\n *   1. Look up the box from the graph.\n *   2. Read each input port's value from its slot (peek mode for\n *      this iteration; pop mode + iterator multi-spawn land later).\n *   3. Do the box's work:\n *        - BOX_CALL — invoke the resolved language spec via the\n *          worker's per-language handle.\n *        - BOX_WRITE — write the `value` input to the path from the\n *          `path` input (or `box->path` if a static literal). Read boxes are\n *          pull-on-demand value sources (issue 244); their cached\n *          bytes are copied directly into a consumer's input buffer\n *          by `read_inputs` when the consumer fires and finds the\n *          slot empty. They are not tasks and never enter the pool.\n *   4. Push the resulting bytes to every outgoing connection's\n *      consumer input slot.\n *   5. For each consumer, fire the spawn-on-input-ready check,\n *      which spawns the consumer iff it has all required inputs\n *      and hasn't been spawned yet (single-spawn guard via an\n *      atomic CAS).\n *\n * The optional `capture_outputs` mode also memcpy's the output\n * bytes into `ctx->last_outputs[box_id]` so tests can verify\n * what each box produced after the pool quiesces.\n *\n * Designed in issue 304.\n */\n\n#include \"012-dispatch.h\"\n#include \"016-unified-allocator.h\"\n\n#include <stdarg.h>\n#include <stdio.h>\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <string.h>\n#include <sys/stat.h>\n#include <time.h>\n\n/* Per-task value buffers (per-input scratch and the output buffer)\n * come from the slot store's unified allocator now, not malloc.\n * This is the dispatch layer's participation in the reference-\n * counted value flow described in issue 302's design retraction:\n * every byte carrying a value through the run passes through the\n * same recycling pipeline, instead of one allocator for slot cells\n * and a separate malloc/free churn for the dispatch's scratch. */"

The resulting directory is portable — copy or symlink it\n# anywhere on the same machine and it runs the map standalone.\n#\n# Layout produced under <map>/compiled/:\n#   meta.json, boxes/, src/, data/  — verbatim copies from the map\n#   langs/<lang>/spec.so            — copies of the language plugins\n#                                     that the map actually uses\n#   langs/bash/bash-server.sh       — only if bash boxes are present\n#   bin/<box>.so                    — pre-compiled C boxes (informational;\n#                                     the runner still lazy-compiles\n#                                     from src/ but having them here\n#                                     means you can verify the compile\n#                                     step worked without running)\n#   pool-runner                     — symlink to soramech-pool\n#   manifest.json                   — summary stats\n#\n# Run as:\n#   scripts/soramech-compile.sh <map-dir>\n#   scripts/soramech-compile.sh <map-dir> --dir <project-root>\n#\n# Convention: scripts run from any directory via a hard-coded ${DIR}\n# path with an override argument; all paths relative to ${DIR}.",

          "description":"Generate 20 read boxes + combine box",
          "command":"cd tests/maps/319a-many-inputs/boxes && python3 -c \"\nimport json\n\n# Generate 20 read boxes, each emitting a number and wiring to combine.in_NN.\nfor i in range(1, 21):\n    label = f'n{i:02d}'\n    port  = f'in_{i:02d}'\n    box = {\n        'id': label,\n        'kind': 'read',\n        'value': str(i),\n        'ui': {'x': 100 + ((i - 1) % 5) * 80, 'y': 100 + ((i - 1) // 5) * 80},\n        'connections': [\n            {'from_box': label, 'from_branch': None,\n             'to_box': 'combine', 'to_input': port}\n        ]\n    }\n    with open(f'{label}.json', 'w') as f:\n        json.dump(box, f, indent=2)\n        f.write('\\n')\n\n# Generate the call box with 20 inputs named in_01..in_20.\ncombine = {\n    'id': 'combine',\n    'kind': 'call',\n    'lang': 'lua',\n    'ref': 'src/many.lua',\n    'fn': 'combine_twenty',\n    'inputs': [\n        {'name': f'in_{i:02d}', 'type': 'string'} for i in range(1, 21)\n    ],\n    'routing': {'kind': 'plain'},\n    'output_capacity': 64,\n    'ui': {'x': 600, 'y': 250}\n}\nwith open('combine.json', 'w') as f:\n    json.dump(combine, f, indent=2)\n    f.write('\\n')\n\nprint('Generated:', sorted(__import__('os').listdir('.')))\n\""
        },
        "caller":{
          "type":"direct"
        },

    "originalFile":"#!/bin/bash\n# scripts/run-tests.sh — phase 3 integration tests.\n#\n# Runs every fixture map under tests/maps/ through `soramech-pool`\n# and asserts that the captured outputs match a hardcoded\n# expectation per map. The point is to catch regressions\n# end-to-end — past the spec interface, past the dispatch action,\n# past JSONL writing — rather than via the in-process unit tests.\n#\n# Per the project convention: scripts run from any directory via a\n# hard-coded ${DIR} path with an override argument; all paths are\n# relative to ${DIR}.\n\nset -u\n\nDIR=\"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech\"\nif [[ $# -ge 1 ]]; then\n    DIR=\"$1\"\nfi\n\ncd \"$DIR\"\n\npass=0\nfail=0\nfailures=()\n\n# {{{ check_map() — run one fixture, verify expected substrings\ncheck_map() {\n    local map=\"$1\"\n    shift\n    local expected=(\"$@\")\n\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"$map\"\n\n    local output\n    output=$(\"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/$map\" 2>&1)\n    local rc=$?\n\n    local missing=\"\"\n    if [[ $rc -ne 0 ]]; then\n        missing=\"exit=$rc\"\n    fi\n    for e in \"${expected[@]}\"; do\n        if [[ \"$output\" != *\"$e\"* ]]; then\n            missing+=\"${missing:+; }missing '$e'\"\n        fi\n    done\n\n    if [[ -z \"$missing\" ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — %s\\n\" \"$missing\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"$map: $missing\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ pipeline_output_check() — additional: the pipeline writes to disk\npipeline_output_check() {\n    local file=\"/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt\"\n    rm -f \"$file\"\n    \"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/pipeline\" > /dev/null 2>&1\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"pipeline write output\"\n    if [[ -f \"$file\" ]]; then\n        local content\n        content=$(cat \"$file\")\n        if [[ \"$content\" == \"11!\" ]]; then\n            printf \"ok\\n\"\n            pass=$((pass + 1))\n        else\n            printf \"FAIL — expected '11!', got '%s'\\n\" \"$content\"\n            fail=$((fail + 1))\n            failures+=(\"pipeline file: $content\")\n        fi\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — output file missing\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"pipeline: $file missing\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ compile_pipeline_check() — soramech-compile produces a portable artifact\n# Verifies issue 309's compile pipeline: bundles all spec.so + sources\n# into compiled/, then runs the artifact from /tmp (i.e. with no\n# dependency on the project's cwd) and verifies it produces the same\n# output as the source map.\ncompile_pipeline_check() {\n    local map=\"$DIR/tests/maps/pipeline\"\n    local compiled=\"$map/compiled\"\n    local file=\"/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt\"\n\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"compile pipeline (portable run)\"\n\n    rm -rf \"$compiled\"\n    if ! \"$DIR/scripts/soramech-compile.sh\" \"$map\" --dir \"$DIR\" >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n        printf \"FAIL — soramech-compile failed\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: script returned non-zero\")\n        return\n    fi\n    if [[ ! -x \"$compiled/pool-runner\" ]]; then\n        printf \"FAIL — compiled/pool-runner missing or not executable\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: pool-runner missing\")\n        return\n    fi\n\n    rm -f \"$file\"\n    local output\n    output=$(cd /tmp && \"$compiled/pool-runner\" \"$compiled\" 2>&1)\n\n    local content=\"\"\n    [[ -f \"$file\" ]] && content=$(cat \"$file\")\n\n    if [[ \"$output\" == *\"addone → 11\"* ]] && [[ \"$content\" == \"11!\" ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — output='%s' file='%s'\\n\" \"$output\" \"$content\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: bad output\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ run all fixtures\necho \"integration tests (fixture maps):\"\n\ncheck_map \"calc\" \\\n    \"add → 42\"\n\ncheck_map \"hello\" \\\n    \"greet → Hello, World!\"\n\ncheck_map \"comparator\" \\\n    \"classify → 8\" \\\n    \"high → HIGH:8\" \\\n    \"low → (no output)\" \\\n    \"mid → (no output)\"\n\ncheck_map \"iter-route\" \\\n    \"iter → hi\" \\\n    \"a → A:hi\" \\\n    \"b → (no output)\" \\\n    \"c → (no output)\"\n\ncheck_map \"pipeline\" \\\n    \"double → 10\" \\\n    \"addone → 11\" \\\n    \"shout → 11!\"\n\ncheck_map \"read-literal\" \\\n    \"echo → hello, world!\"\n\npipeline_output_check\ncompile_pipeline_check\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ parser_tests() — issue 232: unit tests for langs/<lang>/parser.js\n# Run Node's built-in test runner over each per-language parser test\n# file and fold the result into the surrounding pass/fail counters.\n# Each .mjs file is one logical \"test\" from this script's perspective;\n# Node prints its own subtest breakdown on failure for the diagnostic.\nparser_tests() {\n    if ! command -v node >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n        printf \"  %-44s SKIP — node not installed\\n\" \"parser tests (lua, bash)\"\n        return\n    fi\n    for tf in \"$DIR/tests/232-lua-parser-test.mjs\" \\\n              \"$DIR/tests/233-bash-parser-test.mjs\" \\\n              \"$DIR/tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs\"; do\n        local label\n        label=$(basename \"$tf\")\n        printf \"  %-44s \" \"$label\"\n        local out\n        out=$(SORAMECH_DIR=\"$DIR\" node --test \"$tf\" 2>&1)\n        local rc=$?\n        if [[ $rc -eq 0 ]]; then\n            printf \"ok\\n\"\n            pass=$((pass + 1))\n        else\n            printf \"FAIL\\n\"\n            echo \"$out\" | sed 's/^/      /'\n            fail=$((fail + 1))\n            failures+=(\"$label: node --test exit=$rc\")\n        fi\n    done\n}\nparser_tests\n# }}}\n\necho\necho \"  $pass passed, $fail failed\"\n\nif [[ $fail -gt 0 ]]; then\n    echo\n    echo \"  failures:\"\n    for f in \"${failures[@]}\"; do\n        echo \"    - $f\"\n    done\nfi\n\nexit $fail\n",

          "old_string":"## Status\nopen\n\n## Parent issue\nThis is the first slice of issue 319 (built-in library for map\nself-construction). The full design lives in 319; this sub-issue\nimplements the prerequisite from 319's \"Prerequisite — remove the\ndispatch input cap\" section.\n\n## Current behavior\n\n`src/012-dispatch.c` allocates five parallel stack arrays of\nfixed size 16 inside the per-call invocation path (`invoke_box_impl`,\naround lines 804–808, and the parallel set in `do_write_box`,\naround lines 863–866):\n\n```c\nchar        *bufs[16]         = {0};\nua_chunk_t  *buf_chunks[16]   = {0};\nconst void  *datas[16]        = {0};\nint          sizes[16]        = {0};\nint          input_native[16] = {0};\n```\n\nA box with more than 16 inputs hits a hard error (`return -1`)\nfrom the dispatcher with the message `'<id>' has N inputs\n(cap = 16)`. The error is loud, but the cap is arbitrary — it\nexists because someone needed a stack array and picked a number\nthat seemed big enough.\n\nFive additional sites use `char branch[24]` to format\n`\"out_%u\"` strings via `snprintf` (dispatch.c lines 629, 647,\n678, 708, 739). The formatted string is at most 15 bytes\n(`\"out_4294967295\\0\"`), so 24 never truncates, but the\nconstant is arbitrary and the format-string convention is\nimplicit.",
          "new_string":"## Status\ncomplete\n\n## Parent issue\nFirst slice of issue 319 (built-in library for map\nself-construction). The full design lives in 319; this sub-issue\nimplemented the prerequisite from 319's \"Prerequisite — remove\nthe dispatch input cap\" section.\n\n## Current behavior\n\n`src/012-dispatch.c` sizes its per-call input arrays to the box's\nactual input count using C99 VLAs, bounded by a stack-frame\nsanity ceiling `DISPATCH_MAX_INPUTS_PER_BOX` (currently 4096). A\nbox with N inputs gets five parallel arrays of length max(N, 1)\n(the size-1 floor avoids the zero-sized VLA UB; the extra slot\nis never touched because the read loop runs exactly N times).\nBoth `invoke_box_impl()` and `do_write_box()` use the pattern.\n\nThe five branch-name buffers used by the routing kinds\n(comparator, iterator, randomizer, weighted, distributor) share\na single named constant `MAX_BRANCH_NAME` (32 bytes — well above\nthe worst-case `\"out_-2147483648\\0\"` = 16 bytes). Any future\nformat-string change touches one definition.\n\nTest fixture `tests/maps/319a-many-inputs/` exercises a 20-input\nLua call box end-to-end; output `count=20 sum=210` confirms all\n20 values reach the spec."

    "newString":"## Status\ncomplete\n\n## Parent issue\nFirst slice of issue 319 (built-in library for map\nself-construction). The full design lives in 319; this sub-issue\nimplemented the prerequisite from 319's \"Prerequisite — remove\nthe dispatch input cap\" section.\n\n## Current behavior\n\n`src/012-dispatch.c` sizes its per-call input arrays to the box's\nactual input count using C99 VLAs, bounded by a stack-frame\nsanity ceiling `DISPATCH_MAX_INPUTS_PER_BOX` (currently 4096). A\nbox with N inputs gets five parallel arrays of length max(N, 1)\n(the size-1 floor avoids the zero-sized VLA UB; the extra slot\nis never touched because the read loop runs exactly N times).\nBoth `invoke_box_impl()` and `do_write_box()` use the pattern.\n\nThe five branch-name buffers used by the routing kinds\n(comparator, iterator, randomizer, weighted, distributor) share\na single named constant `MAX_BRANCH_NAME` (32 bytes — well above\nthe worst-case `\"out_-2147483648\\0\"` = 16 bytes). Any future\nformat-string change touches one definition.\n\nTest fixture `tests/maps/319a-many-inputs/` exercises a 20-input\nLua call box end-to-end; output `count=20 sum=210` confirms all\n20 values reach the spec.",
    "originalFile":"# 319a — Remove dispatch input cap (prerequisite for create_box)\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Parent issue\nThis is the first slice of issue 319 (built-in library for map\nself-construction). The full design lives in 319; this sub-issue\nimplements the prerequisite from 319's \"Prerequisite — remove the\ndispatch input cap\" section.\n\n## Current behavior\n\n`src/012-dispatch.c` allocates five parallel stack arrays of\nfixed size 16 inside the per-call invocation path (`invoke_box_impl`,\naround lines 804–808, and the parallel set in `do_write_box`,\naround lines 863–866):\n\n```c\nchar        *bufs[16]         = {0};\nua_chunk_t  *buf_chunks[16]   = {0};\nconst void  *datas[16]        = {0};\nint          sizes[16]        = {0};\nint          input_native[16] = {0};\n```\n\nA box with more than 16 inputs hits a hard error (`return -1`)\nfrom the dispatcher with the message `'<id>' has N inputs\n(cap = 16)`. The error is loud, but the cap is arbitrary — it\nexists because someone needed a stack array and picked a number\nthat seemed big enough.\n\nFive additional sites use `char branch[24]` to format\n`\"out_%u\"` strings via `snprintf` (dispatch.c lines 629, 647,\n678, 708, 739). The formatted string is at most 15 bytes\n(`\"out_4294967295\\0\"`), so 24 never truncates, but the\nconstant is arbitrary and the format-string convention is\nimplicit.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nThe five parallel input arrays size themselves at call time to\nthe box's actual input count, with a sanity ceiling that lets us\nreject pathological values (a box with a million inputs is almost\ncertainly a graph-loader bug, not a real use case). No fixed\ncap of 16. A box with 17 inputs runs the same as a box with 7.\n\nThe five branch buffers use a single named constant\n`MAX_BRANCH_NAME` whose size is provably sufficient for the\n`\"out_%u\"` format. The constant lives at file scope so any\nfuture format-string change touches one definition.\n\n## Suggested implementation\n\n1. **Choose the array-sizing approach.** Two acceptable shapes:\n   - **VLA**: `char *bufs[n > 0 ? n : 1]; memset(bufs, 0, sizeof bufs);`\n     for each of the five arrays. C99 standard. Zero stack cost\n     for typical n. Cost: each array gets a tiny init loop;\n     zero-size VLAs are UB so the `n > 0` guard is required.\n   - **SBO**: keep the `[16]` stack arrays as a fast path; fall\n     back to `calloc` when `n > 16`; free at end. Common case\n     pays zero overhead; rare case pays five small allocations.\n\n   Recommended: **VLA** for simplicity. The codebase is C and\n   has no aversion to C99 features. SBO is a fallback if profiling\n   ever shows VLA stack pressure.\n\n2. **Add a sanity ceiling.** Hard-cap n at 4096 (or similar large\n   value). Keep the existing error path; just update the message\n   to name the new ceiling and call out that it's a sanity guard,\n   not a feature limit.\n\n3. **Apply the same change in `do_write_box`** — the parallel\n   arrays there have the same shape, the same cap, and need the\n   same fix.\n\n4. **Introduce `MAX_BRANCH_NAME`** at the top of `dispatch.c`\n   (or in a shared header if it's referenced elsewhere). Replace\n   the five `char branch[24]` / `char want[24]` declarations with\n   `char branch[MAX_BRANCH_NAME]`. Value chosen so that\n   `\"out_4294967295\\0\"` (15 bytes) fits with margin (16 or 32).\n\n5. **Test.** Either:\n   - Add a unit test under `tests/319a-dispatch-vla-test.c` that\n     constructs a box record with > 16 inputs and runs it through\n     the dispatch invocation path, or\n   - Add a test map under `tests/maps/319a-many-inputs/` with a\n     box whose function accepts 20 inputs, exercised by the\n     existing test runner.\n\n   The first option is more isolated; the second is more\n   end-to-end. Probably do both — the unit test catches the change,\n   the map confirms nothing else along the path silently caps.\n\n6. **Build the full test suite** and confirm no existing tests\n   regress.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — the five-array allocation in\n  `invoke_box_impl()` and `do_write_box()`; the five `branch[24]`\n  sites.\n\n## Not in scope for this sub-issue\n\n- Slot store growth (319b).\n- Box id generator / compile cache (319c).\n- The `create_box` / `connect` runtime built-ins themselves\n  (319d, 319e).\n",

          "description":"Commit 319a closeout + design updates",
          "command":"git commit -m \"$(cat <<'EOF'\n319a — closeout: dispatch loses its width ceiling\n\nBoxes no longer cap at 16 inputs. The per-call scratch buffers\nin the dispatch layer were five parallel fixed-size arrays sized\nby guess; they're now sized to the box's actual width at call\ntime, bounded only by a generous stack-frame sanity ceiling.\nThe five branch-name buffers used by routing share a single\nnamed constant in place of a scatter of identical magic\nnumbers.\n\nExtra changes folded into this commit, none behaviour-affecting\non their own:\n\n- The parent issue 319 (built-in library for map self-\n  construction) is committed as a finished design document,\n  with five resolved decisions and a maintained audit list of\n  every per-box toggle the runtime built-ins must accept.\n- Sub-issues 319b–e are committed as planning stubs that hand\n  the next slices off to their own tickets.\n- Issue 248 (encapsulated map as box) is amended to its\n  symmetric-toggle form: data boxes can be marked externally-\n  supplied, write boxes can be marked externally-consumed, and\n  each externally-consumed write box surfaces as a distinct\n  output port on the encapsulating box. The earlier\n  byte-blob packed-output design is rejected and preserved as\n  design history. This makes encapsulated maps the documented\n  exception to the single-output-per-box rule.\n\nA 20-input fixture map exercises the cap removal end-to-end;\nall twelve integration tests pass.\n\nCo-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>\nEOF\n)\" 2>&1 | tail -10"
        },
        "caller":{
          "type":"direct"
        },

```json
{
  "sourceToolAssistantUUID":"8ed0bf3e-426d-4a0f-b960-654a1cdd32e9",

  "parentUuid":"8ed0bf3e-426d-4a0f-b960-654a1cdd32e9",
  "uuid":"0eb747ce-11ef-45bb-b271-4cd1f2a6dfa3",

  "type":"user",
  "toolUseResult":{
    "noOutputExpected":false,
    "stdout":"# 313 — Research: whole-program same-language compilation\n\n## Status\nin progress — Lua slice landed 2026-05-21 (compile-time\nconcatenation in `soramech-compile.sh`, runtime detection in the\nLua spec, end-to-end test). C and Bash merges are follow-ons.\n\n## Concept\n\nInstead of one box = one function call going through the dispatch\nlayer + slot store + spec invocation, **merge all same-language\nboxes at compile time into a single translation unit** for that\nlanguage. Box-to-box transitions within a language region become\nordinary function calls — the optimizer can inline across them, the\nlanguage runtime stays warm, and the slot store and dispatch layer\ndon't run for those transitions at all. Only cross-language wires\nretain the slot machinery.\n\nFor C: every C box becomes a function in one big `.c` file, with\nthe build emitting one `.so`. Wire endpoints become direct calls;\nthe optimizer inlines based on its usual heuristics.\n\nFor Lua: every Lua function gets pre-compiled into one bytecode\nchunk loaded into one shared `lua_State` per worker. Wire\nendpoints become direct `lua_pcall`s into that chunk — no JSON\nencode/decode, no slot push/pop, no spec re-entry per call.\n\nFor Bash: probably no benefit — Bash is already process-per-call;\nfusing scripts doesn't help much. Skip.\n\n## Relationship to 312 — what stays, what thins\n\n312 defines the **wire format**: dual-ring slots (native ring,\nJSON ring, ordering ring) per input port, per-edge classification\nat graph load, JSON-only-at-borders, native-otherwise. Every\nvalue movement between boxes goes through this machinery.\n\nThis issue's merge thins the **spec invocation overhead** — the\ndlsym + bridge + lua_pcall (or equivalent) that happens once\nper box invocation. For boxes in the merged region, the dispatch\nholds a direct pointer to the function inside the merged module\nand calls it without going through the spec interface.\n\nThe slot machinery stays alive in the merged region. Why:\n**boxes still run as separate thread-pool tasks**. A producer\non worker 0 and a consumer on worker 1 still need slots to hand\noff the value across threads. The thread pool's parallelism\ndepends on tasks being scheduled independently; collapsing\nsame-language hops to synchronous function calls would defeat\nthe pool entirely. The merge wins on the per-call indirection\ncost, not on the wire format.\n\nSo a box invocation inside the merged region looks like:\n\n1. Worker picks up the task.\n2. Dispatch reads inputs from the box's slots (same as 312 —\n   dual-ring native side).\n3. Dispatch jumps to the merged function directly (this is\n   what 313 wins).\n4. Function runs, returns a value.\n5. Dispatch writes output to consumer slots (same as 312).\n\nSteps 2 and 5 are unchanged from 312. Step 3 is the savings.\n\n## Why this is research, not a feature\n\nThree open questions that need code-level investigation before\nthe design is concrete:\n\n1. **Loop and iterator boundaries**: a same-language region with an\n   iterator inside it has dynamic re-spawning. Is the iterator\n   merged in (a loop in the generated code) or does it remain a\n   spec-mediated boundary? If the latter, the merge buys less.\n2. **Compile time**: whole-program optimization is slow. Does the\n   incremental-compile model (issue 309's mtime check) still apply,\n   or do edits require a full rebuild of the merged region?\n3. **Debug story**: a stack trace inside the merged region needs to\n   point back to a specific box.         "content":"# 313 — Research: whole-program same-language compilation\n\n## Status\nin progress — Lua slice landed 2026-05-21 (compile-time\nconcatenation in `soramech-compile.sh`, runtime detection in the\nLua spec, end-to-end test). C and Bash merges are follow-ons.\n\n## Concept\n\nInstead of one box = one function call going through the dispatch\nlayer + slot store + spec invocation, **merge all same-language\nboxes at compile time into a single translation unit** for that\nlanguage. Box-to-box transitions within a language region become\nordinary function calls — the optimizer can inline across them, the\nlanguage runtime stays warm, and the slot store and dispatch layer\ndon't run for those transitions at all. Only cross-language wires\nretain the slot machinery.\n\nFor C: every C box becomes a function in one big `.c` file, with\nthe build emitting one `.so`. Wire endpoints become direct calls;\nthe optimizer inlines based on its usual heuristics.\n\nFor Lua: every Lua function gets pre-compiled into one bytecode\nchunk loaded into one shared `lua_State` per worker. Wire\nendpoints become direct `lua_pcall`s into that chunk — no JSON\nencode/decode, no slot push/pop, no spec re-entry per call.\n\nFor Bash: probably no benefit — Bash is already process-per-call;\nfusing scripts doesn't help much. Skip.\n\n## Relationship to 312 — what stays, what thins\n\n312 defines the **wire format**: dual-ring slots (native ring,\nJSON ring, ordering ring) per input port, per-edge classification\nat graph load, JSON-only-at-borders, native-otherwise. Every\nvalue movement between boxes goes through this machinery.\n\nThis issue's merge thins the **spec invocation overhead** — the\ndlsym + bridge + lua_pcall (or equivalent) that happens once\nper box invocation. For boxes in the merged region, the dispatch\nholds a direct pointer to the function inside the merged module\nand calls it without going through the spec interface.\n\nThe slot machinery stays alive in the merged region. Why:\n**boxes still run as separate thread-pool tasks**. A producer\non worker 0 and a consumer on worker 1 still need slots to hand\noff the value across threads. The thread pool's parallelism\ndepends on tasks being scheduled independently; collapsing\nsame-language hops to synchronous function calls would defeat\nthe pool entirely. The merge wins on the per-call indirection\ncost, not on the wire format.\n\nSo a box invocation inside the merged region looks like:\n\n1. Worker picks up the task.\n2. Function runs, returns a value.\n5. Dispatch writes output to consumer slots (same as 312).\n\nSteps 2 and 5 are unchanged from 312.     "content":[{
        "name":"Write",
        "input":{
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/scripts/export-llm-transcripts.sh",
          "content":"#!/bin/bash\n# scripts/export-llm-transcripts.sh — capture this project's Claude\n# conversation history at every verbosity level.\n#\n# What it does, in CEO terms: every conversation Claude has had about\n# this project is stored as a JSONL file under ~/.claude/projects/.\n# An external tool can render those JSONL files into human-readable\n# markdown at six different levels of detail (terse code-only to raw\n# tool-result firehose). This script invokes that external tool once\n# per verbosity level and parks the rendered markdown under\n# llm-transcripts/ so the project repo carries its own development\n# history alongside the code.\n#\n# Intended use: run as part of the commit ritual — refreshes the\n# tracked transcripts so each commit captures the state of project\n# history at that moment.\n#\n# Per the project convention: scripts run from any directory via a\n# hard-coded ${DIR} path with an override argument; all paths are\n# relative to ${DIR}.\n\nset -u\n\nDIR=\"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech\"\nif [[ $# -ge 1 ]]; then\n    DIR=\"$1\"\nfi\n\n# {{{ External exporter location and verbosity table\nEXPORTER=\"/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/scripts/claude-conversation-exporter.sh\"\n\n# Verbosity levels offered by the external tool. Each produces a\n# different lens on the same conversations:\n#   v0 minimal  — code + essentials, useful for \"what was actually written\"\n#   v1 compact  — drops user sentiments\n#   v2 standard — the default, everything readable\n#   v3 verbose  — adds context-file expansions\n#   v4 complete — adds LLM execution detail + vimfolds\n#   v5 raw      — every intermediate step and tool result\ndeclare -A LEVELS=(\n    [0]=\"minimal\"\n    [1]=\"compact\"\n    [2]=\"standard\"\n    [3]=\"verbose\"\n    [4]=\"complete\"\n    [5]=\"raw\"\n)\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Sanity checks\nif [[ ! -x \"$EXPORTER\" ]]; then\n    echo \"error: external exporter not found at $EXPORTER\" >&2\n    exit 1\nfi\n\nif [[ ! -d \"$DIR\" ]]; then\n    echo \"error: project directory not found: $DIR\" >&2\n    exit 1\nfi\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Output directory\nOUT_DIR=\"$DIR/llm-transcripts\"\nmkdir -p \"$OUT_DIR\"\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Run the exporter once per verbosity level\necho \"Exporting LLM transcripts for $DIR\"\necho \"  → $OUT_DIR/\"\n\nfor level in 0 1 2 3 4 5; do\n    name=\"${LEVELS[$level]}\"\n    out_file=\"$OUT_DIR/v${level}-${name}.md\"\n    printf \"  v%d %-10s \" \"$level\" \"$name\"\n\n    if \"$EXPORTER\" \"-v$level\" \"$DIR\" all > \"$out_file\" 2>/dev/null; then\n        size=$(wc -c < \"$out_file\" 2>/dev/null || echo \"?\")\n        printf \"ok (%s bytes)\\n\" \"$size\"\n    else\n        rc=$?\n        printf \"FAIL (exit=%d)\\n\" \"$rc\"\n    fi\ndone\n# }}}\n\necho \"Done.\"\n"
        },
        "caller":{
          "type":"direct"
        },
        "id":"toolu_015mMcXdZyvQiDXSPf6DL3nK",
        "type":"tool_use"
      }],
    "stop_reason":"tool_use",
    "model":"claude-opus-4-7"
  },

This commit lands all of it.\n\nWhat's in the dual-ring shape: each input slot now carries three\nparallel rings (native bytes, JSON bytes, ordering tuples). The\nordering ring records arrival-time `(which_ring, idx)` pairs so a\nconsumer's pop returns cells in arrival order regardless of which\ndata ring each one came from. Same-language producers write to the\nnative ring (no encode cost); cross-language producers write to\nthe JSON ring (decode happens once at the receiver). The per-slot\nspinlock covers all three rings, so a push's data write and its\nordering write are atomic together.\n\nWhat's in the spec contract: a single `invoke` entry point now\ntakes per-input `input_native[]` and per-call `output_native`\nflags. Each spec dispatches per input internally — native bytes\nget pushed as the language's raw form, JSON bytes get decoded.\nOutput side mirrors: native form when the call's consumers are\nall same-language, JSON form when any consumer crosses a boundary.\n\nWhat's in the spec implementations: Lua, C, and Bash all carry\nthe new contract end-to-end. Lua and C grow real JSON in/out\nbridges (Lua via its `cjson`-like encoder using the project's\nJSON library; C via libs/json folded into spec.so). Bash stays\nwith string passthrough since cross-language Bash flows are still\nthe rare case. Spec tests under tests/306-, 307-, 308- exercise\neach side's new shape.\n\nWhat's in the test fixtures: hello.lua gains a `sum_pair` Lua\nfunction that the slice-4 JSON-input test points at; pipeline.lua\nloses an explicit `tostring` so the slice-4.5 output encoder can\nsee the actual Lua number rather than a string-coerced version.\n\nNote on commit boundary: langs/lua/spec.c also carries the\n`load_via_merged` function and its call site, which physically\nbelong to issue 313 (Lua same-language merge). They're committed\nhere because they're interleaved with 312's slice 4 / 4.5 work\ninside `lua_invoke` — the two were developed together and can't\nbe cleanly split without source-level rework. The 313 commit\nthat follows lands the compile-script side that produces the\nmerged module file this opt-in reads.\n\nValidation: all 22 slot-store unit tests pass (including the 5\nnew dual-ring tests); all 12 integration-test maps pass.\n\nCo-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>\nEOF\n)\" 2>&1 | tail -5"
        },
